commentary: The WTI curve is in backwardation: the 12th contract trades 13.2% below the front ($83.08 → $72.08). Prompt barrels are scarcer than future barrels, so the market is paying for oil today. A fully collateralised long-futures position earns roughly the T-bill rate (4.1%) plus a 15.5% annualised roll yield.
Backing out cost-of-carry, the implied net convenience yield (convenience yield minus storage cost) is 19.5% a year: positive, meaning holders of physical crude value having it on hand.
The 3-2-1 crack spread is $36.78/bbl (76th percentile of 3 years, 1-year avg $47.79): refining margins are rich. Valero moves about 32 bp for every $1 change in the crack.

At today's pump price a gasoline car costs 13.0¢/mile to fuel versus 6.1¢ for an EV charged at home and 15.4¢ on a public fast charger. Home charging saves about $693 per 10,000 miles; fast charging only beats the pump when gasoline exceeds $4.30/gal, which maps to roughly $101 WTI through the pass-through regression.

Over the next 12 months, the futures curve prices WTI at $71.91 and USO options imply 42% volatility, giving a 90% risk-neutral range of $33–$131. The options market puts the chance of a 20%+ rally at 16% and a 20%+ drop at 51%. Probability that public fast charging is cheaper per mile than gasoline a year from now: 15%.

Factor model (1y daily, market + oil): oil equities carry an oil beta of 0.28 (t=11.4); EV makers carry -0.00 (t=-0.1) and a market beta of 1.38; charging names -0.04 (t=-0.6). EV stocks do not behave like a short-oil hedge: they trade as high-beta growth equities, so the ‘transition trade’ is mostly a bet on the equity market rather than on oil.

Oil options: USO 30-day implied vol is 42.7% vs 51.5% realised (variance risk premium -8.8 vol pts), an expected ±12.2% one-month move. The 90/110 skew is -0.0 pts: upside calls are bid, so the market is paying up for supply-shock protection.
watch: Rates: 3M T-bill 4.15%, 2s10s +16 bp. Under cost of carry, higher funding rates make holding inventory dearer and push the oil curve toward contango, while rate cuts do the opposite. Easier money also tends to lift long-duration, high-beta EV equities more than cash-generating oil majors.
Curve shape: if the M1–M12 spread flips sign, the market has moved from tight to oversupplied (or the reverse). That is the single most informative daily signal on this page.

Crack spread vs crude: when retail gasoline rises because the crack widened rather than because crude rose, refining margins are doing the work. That matters for the EV cost advantage and for refiner equities.
TSLA implied vol (50%) is the market's price for EV-sector uncertainty; compare it with USO vol to see whether risk is priced in the old energy economy or the new one.
